case_info.explanation: Magnesium and calcium replacement therapy were started immediately. Thiamine was also administered. Clinical evolution was favorable with progressive improvement of symptoms, normalization of metabolic parameters, and radiological resolution of the MRI abnormalities. The lack of family history and the speed of onset and advanced age suggested acquired ataxia. The recent history of arrhythmia and seizures indicated an extraneurological involvement, and the transient episodes of tetaniform rigidity suggested neuromuscular hyperexcitability. Notably, downbeat nystagmus can be caused by lesions at the craniocervical junction, diseases of the lower brainstem and cerebellum, or metabolic disturbances, including vitamin B1, vitamin B12, or magnesium deficiencies.1Therefore, vitamin deficiencies and ionic alterations were considered as explanations for the cerebellar dysfunction and cardiac dysfunction.2However, neuromuscular hyperexcitability with tetaniform rigidity made ionic disturbances the first diagnostic suspicion because of its association with metabolism of calcium and magnesium. The patient’s history of alcohol use could have been associated with toxic effects or vitamin deficiency–related ataxia, but alcohol intake had stopped more than 10 years earlier. The critically low serum magnesium levels explained the progressive mental disorder and cerebellar ataxia, downbeat nystagmus, transient episodes of tetaniform rigidity, seizures, heart failure, cardiac arrhythmia, and general syndrome. The exclusion of other plausible etiologies and the regression of clinical and radiological alterations after magnesium replacement therapy support the diagnosis of reversible cerebellar ataxia associated with hypomagnesemia. This patient was taking 2 drugs that can lower magnesium levels: a PPI and a loop diuretic. The use of PPIs impairs absorption of magnesium by intestinal epithelial cells.3The concomitant use of PPIs and diuretics further increases the risk of hypomagnesemia. PPIs were immediately suspended after hypomagnesemia detection. Hypomagnesemia has been detected in up to 12% of hospitalized patients, and in 60% of patients in the intensive care unit setting.4Its clinical presentation ranges from asymptomatic to life-threatening arrhythmias, and can include neurological symptoms, hypertension, hipocalcemia, and hypokalemia.5Early neurological disturbances include neuropsychiatric problems and neuromuscular hyperexcitability with Chvostek sign, Trousseau sign, tremors, fasciculations, and tetany. It can also cause headaches, seizures, fatigue, and malaise.5 Vertical nystagmus is a rare but diagnostically useful sign of severe hypomagnesemia. In the absence of a structural lesion of the cerebellar and vestibular pathways, the only other recognized metabolic etiology is Wernicke encephalopathy.1However, there was no malnourishment, active alcohol use, or evidence of other predisposing conditions associated with Wernicke encephalopathy, and MRI findings were not typical. The lack of a prompt response to intravenous thiamine administration also countered this diagnosis, although the response to thiamine may be less evident in the presence of hypomagnesemia.6 Hypomagnesemia associated with ataxia and reversible cerebellar hyperintensities has been described on a few occasions.7The typical neuroradiological pattern of hypomagnesemia is characterized by cerebellar hyperintense lesions involving the cerebellar vermis. Lesions restricted to cerebellar nodulus are extremely rare. Isolated nodular infarctions are characterized by an abrupt onset of symptoms, typically isolated vestibular syndrome.8The neuroimaging differs from the MRI presented in this patient because of the presence of characteristic diffusion restriction.8 The pathogenesis of cerebellar dysfunction probably relates to the stabilizing role of magnesium on the vascular endothelium. Critically low magnesium levels mimic the vascular endothelial dysregulation seen in posterior reversible encephalopathy syndrome leading to cerebral edema of the posterior circulation territories.9 Magnesium is not part of the routine electrolyte panel in most hospitals. Hypomagnesemia constitutes a rare and treatable cause of cerebellar ataxia, but one that needs to be specifically thought of. In such cases, early diagnosis and management are essential to avoid permanent cerebellar impairment. Neurologists must be alert to the clinical presentations associated with hypomagnesaemia and the severity of its consequences.

case_info.explanation: Magnesium and calcium replacement therapy were started immediately. Thiamine was also administered. Clinical evolution was favorable with progressive improvement of symptoms, normalization of metabolic parameters, and radiological resolution of the MRI abnormalities. The lack of family history and the speed of onset and advanced age suggested acquired ataxia. The recent history of arrhythmia and seizures indicated an extraneurological involvement, and the transient episodes of tetaniform rigidity suggested neuromuscular hyperexcitability. Notably, downbeat nystagmus can be caused by lesions at the craniocervical junction, diseases of the lower brainstem and cerebellum, or metabolic disturbances, including vitamin B1, vitamin B12, or magnesium deficiencies.1Therefore, vitamin deficiencies and ionic alterations were considered as explanations for the cerebellar dysfunction and cardiac dysfunction.2However, neuromuscular hyperexcitability with tetaniform rigidity made ionic disturbances the first diagnostic suspicion because of its association with metabolism of calcium and magnesium. The patient’s history of alcohol use could have been associated with toxic effects or vitamin deficiency–related ataxia, but alcohol intake had stopped more than 10 years earlier. The critically low serum magnesium levels explained the progressive mental disorder and cerebellar ataxia, downbeat nystagmus, transient episodes of tetaniform rigidity, seizures, heart failure, cardiac arrhythmia, and general syndrome. case_info.explanation: Magnesium and calcium replacement therapy were started immediately. Thiamine was also administered. Clinical evolution was favorable with progressive improvement of symptoms, normalization of metabolic parameters, and radiological resolution of the MRI abnormalities. The lack of family history and the speed of onset and advanced age suggested acquired ataxia. The recent history of arrhythmia and seizures indicated an extraneurological involvement, and the transient episodes of tetaniform rigidity suggested neuromuscular hyperexcitability. Notably, downbeat nystagmus can be caused by lesions at the craniocervical junction, diseases of the lower brainstem and cerebellum, or metabolic disturbances, including vitamin B1, vitamin B12, or magnesium deficiencies.1Therefore, vitamin deficiencies and ionic alterations were considered as explanations for the cerebellar dysfunction and cardiac dysfunction.2However, neuromuscular hyperexcitability with tetaniform rigidity made ionic disturbances the first diagnostic suspicion because of its association with metabolism of calcium and magnesium. The patient’s history of alcohol use could have been associated with toxic effects or vitamin deficiency–related ataxia, but alcohol intake had stopped more than 10 years earlier. The critically low serum magnesium levels explained the progressive mental disorder and cerebellar ataxia, downbeat nystagmus, transient episodes of tetaniform rigidity, seizures, heart failure, cardiac arrhythmia, and general syndrome. The exclusion of other plausible etiologies and the regression of clinical and radiological alterations after magnesium replacement therapy support the diagnosis of reversible cerebellar ataxia associated with hypomagnesemia. This patient was taking 2 drugs that can lower magnesium levels: a PPI and a loop diuretic. The use of PPIs impairs absorption of magnesium by intestinal epithelial cells.3The concomitant use of PPIs and diuretics further increases the risk of hypomagnesemia. PPIs were immediately suspended after hypomagnesemia detection. Hypomagnesemia has been detected in up to 12% of hospitalized patients, and in 60% of patients in the intensive care unit setting.4Its clinical presentation ranges from asymptomatic to life-threatening arrhythmias, and can include neurological symptoms, hypertension, hipocalcemia, and hypokalemia.5Early neurological disturbances include neuropsychiatric problems and neuromuscular hyperexcitability with Chvostek sign, Trousseau sign, tremors, fasciculations, and tetany. It can also cause headaches, seizures, fatigue, and malaise.5 Vertical nystagmus is a rare but diagnostically useful sign of severe hypomagnesemia. In the absence of a structural lesion of the cerebellar and vestibular pathways, the only other recognized metabolic etiology is Wernicke encephalopathy.1However, there was no malnourishment, active alcohol use, or evidence of other predisposing conditions associated with Wernicke encephalopathy, and MRI findings were not typical. The lack of a prompt response to intravenous thiamine administration also countered this diagnosis, although the response to thiamine may be less evident in the presence of hypomagnesemia.6 Hypomagnesemia associated with ataxia and reversible cerebellar hyperintensities has been described on a few occasions.7The typical neuroradiological pattern of hypomagnesemia is characterized by cerebellar hyperintense lesions involving the cerebellar vermis. Lesions restricted to cerebellar nodulus are extremely rare. Isolated nodular infarctions are characterized by an abrupt onset of symptoms, typically isolated vestibular syndrome.8The neuroimaging differs from the MRI presented in this patient because of the presence of characteristic diffusion restriction.8 The pathogenesis of cerebellar dysfunction probably relates to the stabilizing role of magnesium on the vascular endothelium. Critically low magnesium levels mimic the vascular endothelial dysregulation seen in posterior reversible encephalopathy syndrome leading to cerebral edema of the posterior circulation territories.9 Magnesium is not part of the routine electrolyte panel in most hospitals. Hypomagnesemia constitutes a rare and treatable cause of cerebellar ataxia, but one that needs to be specifically thought of. In such cases, early diagnosis and management are essential to avoid permanent cerebellar impairment. Neurologists must be alert to the clinical presentations associated with hypomagnesaemia and the severity of its consequences.
